name: Trapezius
func: The large diamond-shaped muscle of the upper back and neck. It shrugs, squeezes and rotates the shoulder blades, and helps hold up the head and shoulders.

levels.kid:
The **trapezius** is a big, flat muscle on your back. It goes from the back of your head down to the middle of your back and out to your shoulders.

If you look at both sides together, they make a shape like a **diamond** or a kite.

When you **shrug** your shoulders, squeeze your shoulder blades together or lift your arms way up high, your trapezius is working. It also helps hold your head up and keeps your shoulders from slumping. People sometimes call it the "traps".
levels.hs:
The **trapezius** is a broad, flat, triangular muscle lying just under the skin of the back of the neck and upper back. Left and right together form a trapezoid (diamond) shape.

It starts along the midline: the **external occipital protuberance** at the back of the skull, the **nuchal ligament** down the back of the neck, and the spinous processes of vertebrae **C7 to T12**. It inserts on the outer third of the **clavicle**, the **acromion** and the **spine of the scapula**, mirroring the deltoid's origin.

It has three functional parts:
**Upper fibres** elevate the scapula (shrugging) and help rotate it upward.
**Middle fibres** retract the scapula (pull the shoulder blades together).
**Lower fibres** depress the scapula and help rotate it upward.

Upper and lower fibres together with **serratus anterior** rotate the scapula so the glenoid faces upward, which is essential for raising the arm above the head.

Its motor nerve is unusual: the **spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI)**, with sensory (proprioceptive) fibres from C3–C4. Deep to it lie the rhomboids, levator scapulae and the deeper back muscles.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** origin from the medial third of the superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, nuchal ligament, and spinous processes and supraspinous ligaments of C7–T12. Insertion on the posterior border of the lateral third of the clavicle, the medial margin of the acromion and the upper lip of the spine of the scapula (lower fibres converge onto a tubercle near the medial end of the spine).

**Innervation:** the **spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)** arises from the upper cervical cord (spinal nucleus C1–C5), ascends through the foramen magnum, exits the skull through the **jugular foramen**, supplies sternocleidomastoid and then crosses the **posterior triangle of the neck** superficially, lying just under the investing fascia, to reach the deep surface of trapezius. Fibres from the **ventral rami of C3–C4** join it and are mainly proprioceptive, although some may be motor. Blood comes chiefly from the **superficial cervical** (or transverse cervical) artery, plus the dorsal scapular artery and posterior intercostal branches.

**Relations:** the trapezius forms the posterior border of the posterior triangle, and the sternocleidomastoid forms the anterior border. Deep to it lie levator scapulae, rhomboid minor and major, and the splenius and erector spinae muscles. The **triangle of auscultation** is bounded by trapezius, latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula; breath sounds are heard clearly here.

**Scapular force couple:** upward rotation of the scapula is produced by the upper trapezius pulling the acromion up and medially, the lower trapezius pulling the scapular spine down, and serratus anterior pulling the inferior angle forward. Upward rotation contributes roughly a third of the full arc of arm elevation.
levels.phd:
The trapezius's motor supply from a cranial nerve reflects its developmental origin. Classically, it and sternocleidomastoid were thought to derive from **branchiomeric (pharyngeal arch) mesoderm**, which explains why a "cranial" nerve innervates them. Lineage tracing in mice shows a mixed origin: the muscles arise from **lateral plate–adjacent cucullaris precursors** that share genetic programs (for example **Tbx1** and **Isl1** dependence) with pharyngeal arch muscles, while their connective tissue attachments come partly from neural crest. This places them at the head–trunk boundary, a field of active developmental research.

The spinal accessory nucleus is a column of lower motor neurons in the lateral ventral horn of C1–C5/C6. Its axons emerge laterally between the dorsal and ventral roots, a pattern resembling branchial motor neurons. The so-called "cranial root" of CN XI joins the vagus and is now regarded by many as part of the vagus.

Fibre architecture differs regionally. The upper fibres run obliquely and have a small moment arm for scapular elevation but a large one for upward rotation via clavicular leverage. EMG shows the middle and lower parts are recruited strongly during overhead work, while the upper part is tonically active when the arm is held out, for example in keyboard work.

Sustained low-level upper-trapezius activity is studied as a model of **work-related neck–shoulder myalgia**. The "Cinderella hypothesis" proposes that the same low-threshold motor units stay active for long periods without rest, causing local metabolic stress, although evidence is mixed.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** inspect for asymmetry and drooping of the shoulder. Test **shoulder shrug** against resistance (upper fibres) and assess for **lateral scapular winging**, which becomes obvious when the patient abducts the arm. Compare with medial winging from long thoracic nerve injury (serratus anterior), which is best seen when pushing against a wall.

**Spinal accessory nerve injury** is the classic iatrogenic nerve injury of the neck. Because CN XI runs superficially across the posterior triangle, it is vulnerable during **lymph node biopsy**, neck dissection and penetrating trauma. Features: a drooping shoulder, weak shrug and difficulty lifting the arm above shoulder height, with aching pain from the dragging shoulder. EMG confirms denervation. Early nerve repair or grafting gives the best results; late cases may need muscle transfer (the **Eden–Lange procedure** moves levator scapulae and the rhomboids).

**Central versus peripheral:** an upper motor neuron lesion (e.g., stroke) usually produces weakness of the **contralateral** trapezius, while the sternocleidomastoid weakness is often **ipsilateral** to the lesion because its supranuclear control is thought to be largely ipsilateral. A peripheral CN XI lesion weakens both muscles on the **same** side. **Jugular foramen syndrome** (Vernet syndrome) affects CN IX, X and XI together.

**Trapezius myalgia** and **trigger points** are common causes of neck pain and tension-type headaches. In muscular dystrophies (e.g., facioscapulohumeral), the lower trapezius is often weak, with a "trapezius hump" when the arm is raised.

The trapezius flap, based on the transverse cervical artery, is used in reconstruction of the posterior neck and skull base.

keyPoints: Diamond-shaped muscle of the neck and upper back
Upper fibres elevate, middle retract, lower depress the scapula
With serratus anterior, rotates the scapula upward for overhead reach
Motor supply from the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)
CN XI is vulnerable in the posterior triangle → drooping shoulder

test.q: Which nerve provides motor supply to the trapezius?
test.explain: CN XI supplies both trapezius and sternocleidomastoid.

test.q: Which action is mainly performed by the middle trapezius fibres?
test.explain: Middle fibres run horizontally and pull the scapulae toward the spine.

test.q: Which muscle works with trapezius to rotate the scapula upward? (two words)
test.explain: Serratus anterior pulls the inferior angle forward while trapezius pulls the acromion up.

test.q: A lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck is followed by a drooping shoulder and weak shrug. Which nerve was injured?
test.explain: CN XI runs superficially across the posterior triangle.

test.q: The trapezius, latissimus dorsi and scapula bound the triangle of ______.
test.explain: Fewer muscle layers here make breath sounds easy to hear.
